How AI coding plan pricing actually works

Every flat-rate AI coding plan — Claude Pro/Max, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT Plus — is really a bet the vendor is making about your usage against what the same work would cost billed per token. Whether that bet pays off for you depends on numbers neither pricing page shows side by side.

Why cache reads are the number that decides it

An agentic coding session does not send one prompt and get one reply. It resends the system prompt, the tool definitions, the files it has already read, and most of the prior conversation on nearly every turn, because the model has no memory between calls otherwise. Providers that support prompt caching bill that repeated, unchanged block at a small fraction of the fresh-input rate — often around a tenth — specifically because it costs the provider far less to serve a cache hit than to reprocess the same tokens from scratch.

Publicly reported breakdowns of heavy Claude Code usage put cache reads above 90% of total tokens processed, with fresh input and output together under a few percent. A calculator that multiplies "tokens" by one blended rate treats a cache read as if it cost as much as fresh input, which overstates the API-equivalent cost by a large factor for exactly the heavy users who are the ones actually asking "is my plan worth it?" That is why this calculator asks for fresh input, output, cache write, and cache read separately.

The two things a subscription is actually pricing

ModelWhat you're really buying
Flat-rate planA usage allowance (often soft, reset-based, or "fair use") at a fixed monthly price, regardless of your actual token mix. The vendor is pooling risk across many users' usage patterns.
Pay-per-token APIExactly what you use, at published per-token rates, with no allowance to hit or reset to wait out — but no ceiling either if usage spikes.

Neither is "correct" on its own — a light user well under a plan's allowance is very likely leaving money on the table by paying the flat rate; a heavy user who keeps hitting a five-hour usage reset is very likely leaving money on the table too, in the form of blocked time the API model would not have cost them. The calculator's break-even figure is the usage level where the two cross for your own numbers.

What happens after the allowance runs out

The comparison above quietly assumes the flat fee buys unlimited usage. For a light user it does. For the heavy agentic user actually asking this question it usually does not, and the error runs one way: treating a metered plan as unlimited always flatters the subscription, because it books the overflow at nothing.

Enter an allowance in the calculator's optional field and the plan side gets an honest total — the flat fee, plus whatever runs past the allowance priced at the same API rates as the other column. It also names the active day you exhaust it on, which is often the more useful number: "you run out on day 14" tells you something a monthly average hides.

That changes the shape of the break-even question, and the answer is not intuitive. Below the allowance, growing usage pushes the API column up while the plan stays flat, so the two cross somewhere — that is the usual break-even. Above it, both columns grow at exactly the same per-token rate, so the gap between them stops moving. It settles at the value of your allowance at those rates, minus what you pay for it. Past that point more usage does not change the answer at all: the only things that move it are the rates and the size of the allowance.

One consequence worth naming, because it is the whole decision for a heavy user: if your allowance is worth less at API rates than the fee you pay for it, no amount of extra usage will ever make the plan win. The usual advice to "use it more to get your money's worth" is only true up to the ceiling.

The calculator ships no default allowance for any named plan, on purpose. Vendors publish these limits in messages, "premium requests", or rolling five-hour windows — not in tokens — so there is no sourced figure to pre-fill, and a made-up one would be worse than an empty field. Your own estimate, from your own usage, is the number that belongs there.

Seats change the comparison, not just the total

Business and team subscription tiers are priced per seat, and the API-equivalent side scales with actual usage, not headcount — a team where three of five seats are light users is a very different comparison from one where all five run agentic loops most of the day. Enter the seat count that matches your plan and let the usage fields reflect a typical member, or run the calculator once per usage band if your team is uneven.

Check the numbers yourself before deciding

List prices and API rates in the calculator are dated defaults, not a live feed — nothing on this page makes a network call, so it cannot know about a price change the moment it happens. Before switching plans on the strength of a result here, check the vendor's own current pricing:

  • Anthropic — Claude plans and API pricing
  • Cursor — plan pricing
  • GitHub Copilot — plan pricing
  • OpenAI — API pricing

Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Anthropic, Cursor, GitHub, Microsoft, or OpenAI. Each is a trademark of its respective owner, named here only to point to their own published pricing.

Questions

Why do cache reads matter so much more than input or output tokens?

An agentic coding session resends the system prompt, the tool definitions, the files it has already read, and most of the prior conversation on nearly every turn, because the model has no memory between calls otherwise. Providers that support prompt caching bill that repeated, unchanged block at a small fraction of the fresh-input rate, and publicly reported breakdowns of heavy Claude Code usage put cache reads above 90% of total tokens processed.

Is a subscription always cheaper for a heavy user?

Not automatically. It depends on the plan price, the model's API rates, and how many of your tokens are cheap cache reads versus expensive fresh input and output. A heavy user whose sessions are mostly cache reads can still come out ahead on the API for some models and plans, which is why the calculator asks for your own numbers rather than assuming a verdict.

Do seats change which option is cheaper?

Yes. Business and team subscription tiers are priced per seat, and the API-equivalent side scales with actual usage, not headcount, so a team with uneven usage across seats is a different comparison from a single heavy user. Enter the seat count that matches your plan and a typical member's usage, or run the calculator once per usage band.

How current are the default prices and rates?

They are dated defaults recorded because this page makes no network call, not a live feed, and vendors change pricing without notice. Check the vendor's own current pricing page before switching plans on the strength of a result here.

No warranty. This page and the linked calculator produce estimates from numbers you supply — they are not financial advice and not a quote from any vendor. Verify anything here against the vendor's own pricing page before acting on it.

AI CODING PLAN COST CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Is your AI coding plan cheaper than the API — or is the API cheaper than your plan?

Vendor pricing pages quote a flat monthly price on one page and a per-token API rate on another, and never do the multiplication for how you actually use the tool. This does — enter your plan, your usage, and the model's rates (or start from a preset and edit it), and it works out both monthly costs and the usage level where they cross.

Nothing is uploaded. Every number here stays in this browser.

1. Your subscription

Leave the allowance blank and this compares a flat fee against the API, which is the right shape only if your plan never cuts you off. If yours does, put your own estimate of the monthly token allowance in — usage past it is priced at the same API rates as the other column, and the result will tell you which day of the month you run out. There is no default here on purpose: vendors publish these limits in messages, “premium requests”, or rolling five-hour windows, never in tokens, so any figure we pre-filled would be invented rather than sourced.

2. Your usage (per active day)

Cache reads usually dwarf everything else in an agentic coding session — most of the context is the same files and history sent again, billed at a fraction of the fresh-input rate. If you don't know your numbers, pick a starting point above and adjust it.

3. API rates it would cost to run that usage yourself

Picking a plan above also switches this to that vendor's own API rates — Claude for Claude and Cursor plans (Cursor runs several models; Claude is the closest single default, and Gemini is also here as a preset if that's what you actually run through it), OpenAI's API for ChatGPT Plus and GitHub Copilot. Anthropic charges extra to write to its prompt cache and less to read it back; OpenAI and Google do not bill the write step at all, only a discounted read, which the two new presets model as a $0 cache-write rate.

Why this differs from a simple "tokens × price" calculator

Most cost calculators multiply input and output tokens by a blended rate and stop. That understates the case for a subscription for exactly the users asking this question: agentic coding tools resend most of the file and conversation context on almost every turn, and providers that support prompt caching bill that repeated, unchanged prefix at a small fraction of the fresh-input rate. Questions

Is Claude Max actually worth it over the API?

It depends entirely on how much you use it and how much of that usage is cache reads, which are billed far below fresh input on providers that support prompt caching. This calculator takes your own token estimates (or a light/typical/heavy starting point you edit) and the plan's price, and reports which is cheaper this month and at what usage level the other one would catch up.

Why does this ask for cache read and cache write tokens separately?

Agentic coding tools resend most of the conversation and file context on nearly every turn. Providers that support prompt caching bill a repeated, unchanged prefix at a small fraction of the fresh-input rate, and publicly reported usage breakdowns for heavy coding-agent use put cache reads above 90% of total tokens. A calculator that only multiplies input and output tokens by a blended rate significantly overstates the API-equivalent cost for exactly the heavy users asking this question.

Where do the default prices and rates come from?

They are list prices and published API rates as of the date shown on the page, recorded here because this tool makes no network call. Vendors change pricing without notice and this calculator cannot know when that happens — every field is a plain number you can edit, and the result is only as current as what you put in. Check the vendor's own pricing page before deciding.

What if my plan has a usage limit?

Put your own estimate of the monthly token allowance in the optional field and the comparison stops assuming the plan is unlimited: usage past the allowance is priced at the same API rates as the other column, the result names the active day you run out on, and an all-in row adds the overflow to the flat fee. There is deliberately no default, because vendors publish coding-plan limits in messages, premium requests, or rolling five-hour windows rather than in tokens, so any figure pre-filled here would be invented rather than sourced. Leave it blank and the plan is treated as unlimited, which is the right shape only if yours never cuts you off.

No. All arithmetic happens in your own browser. There is no account, no server call, and no analytics vendor.

This calculator vs. checking pricing pages yourself

Checking pricing pages yourself gets you the sticker prices: a flat monthly plan price on one page, and per-token API rates on another. That is a fine first step, and it is enough if all you want is the headline numbers. It does not answer the question that actually decides whether the plan is worth it: given your usage, which option is cheaper this month, and how far would that usage need to move before the answer flips.

This calculator takes the same numbers a pricing-page lookup gives you — the plan price, and the four separate API rates for input, output, cache write, and cache read tokens — plus your own token counts (or a light/typical/heavy starting point if you don't know them), and does the comparison arithmetic and the break-even math for you. It doesn't replace reading the pricing pages; the rates it starts you from come straight from them. It replaces the multi-step arithmetic afterward.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I just want to see the sticker prices — the plan cost, or the per-token API rates. The vendor's own pricing page — that quick lookup is exactly its job.
I want to know whether my plan is actually cheaper than the API for how I use it, and by how much. This calculator — runs the four-rate, four-token comparison against your own numbers instead of a blended guess.
I want to know how much my usage would need to change before the cheaper option flips. This calculator — reports the break-even usage level, which a pricing page has no way to tell you.
I don't know my own token counts and don't want to dig them up first. This calculator's light/typical/heavy presets — a starting point you edit, not a blank form.

In practice most people do both: check the vendor's pricing page for the current rates, then bring those numbers here instead of multiplying four rates by four token counts by hand and hoping the cache-read weighting didn't get lost along the way.

Common questions

Why not just check the plan's pricing page and the API pricing page myself?

You can, and the sticker prices alone take thirty seconds to find. What they don't give you is the answer to the actual question: given how much you personally use the tool, which one is cheaper, and by how much would your usage need to change for that to flip. That requires four separate API rates (input, output, cache write, cache read), your own token counts across the same four categories, and the arithmetic to compare a flat monthly number against a usage-weighted one. Most people stop at the sticker prices because the rest is tedious to do by hand, not because it doesn't matter.

What does this calculator do that reading two pricing pages doesn't?

It runs the arithmetic you'd otherwise do by hand: multiplies your input, output, cache write, and cache read tokens by the matching API rate, compares the total to your plan's flat price, and reports the break-even usage level -- how far your usage would need to move before the cheaper option changes. It also starts you from a light/typical/heavy usage preset if you don't already know your own token counts, which most people checking pricing pages by hand don't.

Pricing pages already show cache pricing. Why does doing this by hand still miss it?

The rate is on the page; the mistake is in the mental math, not the lookup. Publicly reported usage breakdowns for heavy agentic coding put cache reads above 90% of total tokens processed, because these tools resend most of the file and conversation context on nearly every turn. A back-of-envelope estimate that blends input and output at a single rate -- the shortcut most people take when doing this by hand -- significantly overstates the API-equivalent cost for exactly the heavy users asking the question. Keeping four rates and four token counts straight through a multi-step comparison is exactly the kind of arithmetic a calculator does more reliably than a person doing it in their head.

Is anything I enter here uploaded?

No. All arithmetic happens in your own browser, the same as if you were doing it on paper -- there is no account, no server call, and no analytics vendor. The only difference is the calculator does not mis-add the columns.

You are responsible for checking any figure here against the vendor's own current pricing page before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Everything you enter is compared locally, exactly like doing the arithmetic on paper -- never uploaded, no account, no analytics vendor.

Free and open source. The code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-doing-the-math-yourself.html.text:
← back to the calculator

This calculator vs. doing the math yourself

Several blog posts already answer "is my AI coding plan worth it?" by hand, from one account's own token counts — one reports ten billion tokens across eight months of Claude Code usage that would have cost $15,000 on the API against an $800 subscription bill, with cache reads above 90% of the total. That arithmetic is real and worth reading. It is also not your arithmetic.

What each one is for

A blog post or forum thread working the numbers by hand reports one account's result: a specific seat count, a specific usage tier, a specific cache-read share, computed once and published. Reading a few of these gives a useful sense of the shape of the answer — subscriptions tend to win big for heavy, cache-heavy usage — but no two accounts split their tokens the same way, and none of these posts let you swap in your own numbers.

This calculator runs the identical subscription-vs-API arithmetic — fresh input, output, cache write, and cache read priced separately, because cache reads are typically billed at a fraction of the fresh-input rate and dominate real agentic-coding usage — from the usage and rates you enter, and reports the break-even point where the two would swap places.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What does this generally look like for a heavy coding-agent user?The published write-ups — a useful sanity check before you dig into your own numbers.
Is my plan cheaper than the API, given my own usage?This calculator — your numbers, not a published account's.
How much would my usage need to change to flip the answer?This calculator's break-even figure, computed rather than a second round of hand arithmetic.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Anthropic, Cursor, GitHub, Microsoft, or OpenAI. Each is a trademark of its respective owner, named here only to describe the plans this calculator compares.

Common questions

Why not just read one of the blog posts that already worked this out?

Those posts are real and useful as a sanity check — several report figures like ten billion tokens across eight months of Claude Code usage costing $15,000 on the API against an $800 subscription bill, with cache reads above 90% of the total. But every one of those numbers comes from one specific account's usage. Your seat count, your usage tier, and your cache-read share are almost certainly different, and none of those posts let you substitute your own numbers — they report what happened to someone else.

Can I just scale a blog post's numbers to my own usage?

Only roughly, and it is easy to get wrong in a way that favors the wrong answer. The ratio between subscription and API cost is not linear in total tokens — it depends on how your usage splits across fresh input, output, cache write, and cache read, and cache reads are typically billed at a small fraction of the fresh-input rate. Scaling someone else's total by your rough usage multiple ignores that split entirely, which is exactly the shortcut this calculator exists to skip.

What does doing this by hand actually involve?

Opening your plan's pricing page for the monthly price, opening the vendor's separate API pricing page for four different per-token rates, estimating your own fresh input, output, cache write, and cache read tokens, and multiplying each rate by its token count before summing and comparing to the subscription price — then redoing all of it if you want to know how much your usage would need to change to flip the answer. It is arithmetic anyone can do; it is also easy to drop a rate, use last month's price, or skip the break-even step because it takes another round of multiplication by hand.

Is this calculator's answer more trustworthy than my own spreadsheet?

Not automatically — it runs the same arithmetic you could run yourself, with the same dated default rates you should still verify against the vendor's current pricing page. What it changes is friction: the four-rate, cache-split arithmetic is filled in for you and the break-even usage level is computed rather than left as a second calculation, so there is one less place to drop a term or forget a step.
